name: Reverse osmosis water filter (under sink)

comps.spec: RO membrane. Holds back most dissolved salt, but makers don't promise it stops germs, so boil what it makes (Pentair RO-2550, DuPont TW30). Feed 2.75–6.9 bar (Pentair RO-2550); DuPont tests at 3.4 bar, where a 50 GPD membrane makes about 190 L a day, and allows 10 bar max (DuPont TW30)
Sediment and carbon-block pre-filters in standard 10 in (25 cm) housings
Granular activated carbon in the inline post-filter
comps.loc: Small inline cartridge before the faucet

comps.spec: Pressurised storage tank with a bladder, 8–15 litres
comps.loc: Under the sink beside the filters

comps.spec: 24V DC diaphragm booster pump (pumped models) — a handy small pump
24V power supply for the booster pump
24V inlet solenoid valve and automatic shut-off valve
UV-C sterilising lamp stage (some models) — never look at it lit
comps.loc: Metal tube on the outlet line

comps.spec: 1/4 in food-grade tubing and push-fit fittings

notes: A header tank gives far too little pressure for the membrane; feed it with the 24V booster pump or another pressure pump. Change used pre-filters: old cartridges grow bacteria. A membrane left to dry out after use loses much of its performance. Don't count on the membrane for germs: Pentair says not to use its unit on unsafe water without disinfection before or after, and DuPont doesn't guarantee its membrane removes cysts and pathogens (Pentair RO-2550, DuPont TW30). Boil the water it makes. Pentair also says to protect the filter from freezing, which can crack it and cause leaks (Pentair RO-2550), so look a unit from a cold building over for cracks.
